utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you have a matter to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three very short matters. The Court was good enough to indicate last -- yesterday afternoon that it would make rulings about the admissibility of certain documents subject to any objections. I have no objections to make; although, I obviously may ask questions of the witness about the source of intelligence material and why we haven't been provided with original materials, and depending on the answers, I might have further submissions to make later. But subject to that reservation, I don't object to the production of these documents. The second point that I think it prudent to mention now, rather than later, is that we're going to be -- we've been provided informally and you're going to be provided, I think, formally with an up-to-date witness list for the accused. The next three witnesses include one of whom we've been given notice and a 65 ter, but also two other witnesses, who although they appeared on the accused's witness list, appeared by pseudonyms with, in reality, no 65 ter of any value. We received their names for the first time yesterday, and accordingly provision of names that late and in these circumstances without any 65 ter makes it difficult for us to perform our task adequately, and there's no explanation for why they've been interposed at this late stage, and the Chamber may wish to consider that. We observe that preparations have been in hand for months now to call another witness, Bulatovic, who we were expecting to be coming and for whom, I think, all documents are now available and those documents being less in quantity than was originally expected. The reason I raise these matters now rather than at any later stage is that personally it would be of great assistance to me to be able to leave the courtroom today at half past 1.00. If the Court doesn't -- assuming that it's still examination-in-chief, which I think it will be, I'm, of course, content to ensure that there's somebody here to continue the process of listening to the evidence and taking a note, unless the Court thought in all the circumstances it would be appropriate to rise at half past 1.00. But I'm in your -- in the Court's hands as to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We think you should have somebody on hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll have somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But because I could see that procedural matters might arise at the end of the day in the way that they sometimes do and then stretch, I thought it better to raise these matters now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And you are right that we are going give a ruling on the admission of some Delic documents. These are documents which were dealt -- which were dealt with in evidence but in respect of which no application was made for their admission. And I am to say that firstly these relate to tabs of Exhibit D300. The tabs for which translations have been provided are admitted into evidence. The tabs for which translations have not been provided are marked for identification pending translation and further order of the Trial Chamber, and these are tabs 64 to 92, tab 204, tab 216, tabs 251 to 253, tab 256, tabs 258 to 260, 292 to 295, 297 to 340, and 343 to 358. And the Prosecution is put on notice that it may make any submissions it wishes. But I understand no opposition is being offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, subject obviously to anything that arises in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, okay. Very well. Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps there's some misunderstanding involved, but it was my understanding that as far as all the tabs so far are concerned, those that are included in your binder that we've dealt with, I asked for all of them to be admitted into evidence in groups, following your instructions that we should move faster through the tabs, and that is why I tendered them in groups on several occasions, groups of tabs that pertained to work with the verification mission, asking the witness only to deal with them very quickly. But all of these documents are valid documents, and I think that they should all be admitted into evidence, up to 359, the one that we've reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, you are right, and we have admitted them. You are right that you -- you had indicated that you are going to deal with them in groups, and I had approved that method of proceeding. The ruling which we have given is to clarify the -- the matter. Yes, please proceed. Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me make it clear. We have admitted all the documents, in case you're not clear. But there was some confusion, I think, arising from dealing with them in groups, but we have admitted the -- the documents. So we have marked for identification those which were not translated. Yes, you may begin, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, yesterday we broke off at the document marked 359. Could you please find it, because I'd like to put a few questions to you with regard to that document.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I am going to dwell on a few elements of this analysis because it goes to this entire operation that you have described already. You showed us the working maps. You told us what it represented. So this is an analysis of activities of the forces under your control from the 25th until the 29th of March, 1999, when many parts of the territory were operated on; that is to say, where the terrorist forces were. Is that that analysis of yours?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In point 1 of your analysis, you say -- or rather, you refer to many villages. I draw your attention to these villages because many of them appear in different testimonies and in the indictment, so we will deal with them in greater detail later. But you say here that "During the operations, the overall strength of the Siptar terrorist forces was estimated at 1.500 terrorists." Is that what you establish in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was our estimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had against you about 1500 of them. Then you refer to the position of the command, that is to say, in the village of Retimlje, set up barracks, a clinic ready to admit 500 persons. And then in the next paragraph, you're dealing with something else, and I want to ask you about that. You say: "Within the context of the defence organisation, it is typical that there was no civilian population in the villages of Retimlje, Studencani and Opterusa, only members of the Siptar terrorist forces." That is what you established.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say that "The Siptar terrorist forces during the operations did not abandon weapons and combat equipment until the crucial moment when they would change into civilian clothes and attempt to break through in the direction of," et cetera, et cetera. So what happened there? What was this all about? Can you explain this a bit better?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said yesterday that there were several units there from my brigade, that there were two lines of blockade: One along the asphalt road Prizren-Djakovica and the other one here, the village of Srbica, then east of Mamusa, Lestane, Trnje, towards Suva Reka. The operations were from Amovac, then the direction of Orahovac, Velika Hoca, and the direction of Suva Reka -- or rather, the village of Rastane in order to link up these two units and in order to deal with the Siptar terrorist forces that were throughout the region. I already said that we could not do that in the morning because the villages of Studencani and here the village of Avdelsa [phoen] there were forces, terrorist forces that were putting up strong resistance and other terrorist forces too, from Dobrodeljan and Grab and here from the -- slopes of Mount Milanovac. We thought that these were terrorists forces that came to their assistance from the direction of Malisevo, so it took us three days to link up our forces. During the operations that started on the 25th, that is to say, in these directions, the first resistance was put up in these combat groups, as you can see here on the map. It was given from this line here, Brestovac, Nogovac, Celine, Velika Krusa, Mala Krusa. And as for the direction of Suva Reka, resistance was put up immediately. On the exit of the village of Rastane, Studencani. And in that direction, our units did not manage to advance at all on that day, only about 500 metres. It is characteristic that in these areas there was very strong resistance. Even the OSCE established in their reports that the terrorist forces fortified their positions there at the third level. "The third level" means that they have trenches that are totally dug in, which enables long-term fighting. As for Velika Krusa, Mala Krusa, Nogovac and Brestovac, our forces managed up to around 12.00 to take this area and to get out of the built-up areas. In all these operations and even when moving through these villages, there weren't any civilians there. The civilian population was not there. And as we can see here in these reports, on the 25th of the afternoon -- or only on the 26th the civilian population was observed here in the area where these brooks were. And as for Velika Hoca, already on the previous day or perhaps in the early morning hours the population went in the direction of Mamusa -- or rather, in Mamusa on the 28th there was already a big concentration of the population. Mamusa probably has a population of -- well, it's a predominantly Muslim population but the regular population is between four and five thousand persons, but there were two times as many people there at that point in time. The civilians had doubled by then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your forces enter Mamusa?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on the 28th in Mamusa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any fighting there, any clashes?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Mamusa. To the west of Mamusa, that is, where the crushed groups were of 10 to 15 people, and also here in the area of Neprebiste, but in Mamusa itself there hadn't been any fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you: Was that an answer to the question that was asked? Because if it was, I fail to understand it. The question related to a passage in your analysis about the Siptar terrorists not abandoning weapons and combat equipment until the crucial moment when they changed into civilian clothing and attempted to break through. Now, that was the question. Did you deal with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This statement is something to which I have nothing to add. I abide by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have I misunderstood the question, Mr. Milosevic? Because we've just spent almost five minutes on an answer that didn't seem to have anything to do with the question. Or do you not intend to follow this up?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It did have a lot to do with the question because in this passage, we can conclude that the resistance was very persistent, and the general explained that the fighting went on for a long time as you can see, from the 25th to the 29th, because of the persistent resistance. They gave up only when it was quite clear they had lost, and that's what he explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, General, you go on to say here that you estimate the Siptar terrorist losses to be about 85.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, that's our estimate according to the commander's reports, the intensity of the fighting, and so on; although, the terrorists, as they had done before, pulled out most of their dead with them. Later on in the fighting that followed later in the area of Pagarusa we found 30 fresh graves where the terrorists were buried, and we assumed that these were men killed in this fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what was the extent of your losses, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On our side, as for my own units, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. three killed and eight wounded. The MUP units also had losses, but I cannot say with certainty. I think there were five killed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, let me draw your attention to page 2 near the bottom in the Serbian version, where it says: "In the course of carrying out the tasks, three of our men were killed and eight wounded." It's contained in this analysis, the answer of General Delic to your question, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask you, General, for a comparison between your weaponry and the weaponry of the -- of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can draw a comparison. As for artillery weapons, we had almost the same weapons. They were even made in the same way. It was the Kalashnikov type and theirs were made in China. The most recent ones were made in Albania. As for sniper weapons, the terrorists had more modern and better weapons than the army had. As for hand-held launchers, the terrorists had RPG-7, which is the Chinese version of the Russian RPG-7 system. It's extremely good. It's used all over the world, even today. As for rocket launchers, they had German Armbrust ones. We had the domestic ones, Zolja. As for mortars, they had the same kind we had, 60, 82 millimetres, and 120 millimetres. They had recoilless guns of American origin, 76 millimetres, which were both recoilless guns and could be used as support weapons because they had some kind of device. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you had an advantage, it would have been in numbers. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The advantage was not in numbers; it was only in anti-armour means and artillery. Artillery was used selectively, and they did not have such -- so much of an advantage. The greatest advantage they had was in the anti-armour weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be in the -- the translation that there are distinctions between what's on the document and what you've said, but your document indicates you had 21 tanks. Did the Albanians have tanks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I've been saying. They -- or rather, they did not have tanks. They did not have armoured -- weapon armour. Tanks belong to armour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next item referred to is what's called Howitzers. Now, have you used a different expression for a Howitzer, or did they have the equivalent of what's here described as a Howitzer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they did not have an equivalent of that calibre, but they did have support weapons. Our Howitzers are 122 millimetres. They had 76-millimetre weapons for support. These were the American recoilless guns which have a range when they are used for support up to 7.100 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these -- well, the next category described here is what's called 30-millimetre PATs, anti-aircraft guns. Did they have these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. As for such weapons, they had 127-millimetre machine-guns and they had Brownings, DSK Brownings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were much better equipped than they were, in terms of weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were a state army. They were terrorists and rebels. Of course, we had all the equipment our state could provide. But as for manpower levels, we were inferior in manpower levels. They had twice as many men as we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In that particular area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's well known that in that area there was only my brigade. At the beginning of the war, it had somewhere around three and a half to four thousand. It's in the reports. The numbers were three and a half to four thousand men. On the territory, only in the area of Suva Reka, in the areas of Budakovo and Studencani, there were about 3.000 terrorists. If we add to this the remainder of my area, the terrorist forces had twice as many men. If we add to this the local village guards, which varied in numbers from 30 to 50 men, depending on the village, then we arrive at a number which shows that the terrorists had a considerable advantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you about this estimate of the number killed, where you say about 85, because in Mr. Nice's allegations there are various numbers pertaining to some sort of victims among the civilian population and the numbers are roughly similar. So I'll ask you this, General: Did you have any knowledge of victims among the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer yet. Mr. Milosevic, point us to the allegations so that we can look at the indictment where 85 is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll come to that specifically. I am just now approaching this analysis in general terms, and you will see there are mentions of 12 or 60, but we'll come to that. We'll come to specific issues. But these are in general numbers that correspond. But you can see from the General's report here that these were terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. But we -- but if you are dealing with a specific allegation in the indictment, then you must bring that to our attention so we can look at the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Robinson. I assume that Mr. Kwon can assist you. In the South Korean elite division, which is considered to be the best in their army, managed to achieve losses of 1 to 150. Here it's less than 1 to 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: See, you have now enlisted Judge Kwon to assist you. Is this 66 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggested that he give you this information so that you can gain an impression of this because I have the impression that you're surprised by certain figures, which should not be surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, please bear this analysis in mind because we might need it when dealing with certain specific issues. But in order to proceed as expeditiously as possible, we shall now deal with the village of Bijela Crkva, which is in the Orahovac municipality as well, to see what the army did in Bijela Crkva. You have a map in document number 360.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume, Mr. Robinson, that you understand I'm asking this analysis to be tendered into evidence. I mean, 359.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Document 360 is a map of Bijela Crkva. What does the map represent and could you please explain it.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you right away that this is a map showing my decision, which was created when preparing to carry out this task. As for this map, this map was created later, in 2000. It was created in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 2002, interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when the Commission for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal summoned all the commanders and took from the indictment all the villages mentioned, not just on my territory but throughout Kosovo and Metohija. They gave us such excerpts from maps, like this one, and asked for an explanation of each particular event. And this was sometime in 2002 or early 2003. This map clarifies the work of my unit, Combat Group 2, which from Djakovica -- or rather, Babaj Boks arrived to Bijela Crkva area. From this axis, they were to carry out a blockade and then proceed to launch an attack on the terrorist forces of the 124th Brigade. On the map, you can see the column of this unit, which around 4.30 was in the village of Zrze and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you put it on the ELMO, this map, when you're explaining so that we can see exactly what you are talking about. In the meantime, while we are waiting for the map to be put on the ELMO, can you just say what the purpose of all these detailed analyses was that were carried out in 2002 and 2003.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of all these analyses, I don't know whether it was done at the request of the legal advisors, but it was done pursuant to orders from the General Staff. The commission, which numbered around 40 people at the time and comprised several academicians and people with Ph.Ds and they were to explain the situation in Kosovo and Metohija on the basis of the documentation, and they were to interview all the commanders who could provide information about the places mentioned in the indictment. So this includes all the places we will talk about, Bijela Crkva, Landovica, Celine, and so on. In early 2003, pursuant to a decision by the new minister, this commission was disbanded. It was dissolved. And through the National Council it presented documentation for the needs of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Through this commission, documents were sent for the needs of Mr. Nice's office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later on there were only five technical staff left in that commission after the first half of 2003.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 66(b) of the indictment, it is alleged that: "On or about the 25th of March, 1999 forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded and attacked the village of Bijela Crkva, Orahovac municipality." That's what it says here. And then we'll -- I'll ask you the following: General, you have just explained this map. On the 18th of December, 2002 you made a statement to the commission you have just mentioned, and this statement is in tab 361, and it refers to information about the alleged crimes in Bijela Crkva. And you signed this statement. Could you say something about this statement, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, on the 25th, I passed through Bijela Crkva because I had set out sometime after 4.00 a.m., perhaps after 0430 hours, on the direction of Landovica, Zrze and so on. I passed through Bijela Crkva, where I saw my unit that had arrived from Djakovica. It was already passing through Bijela Crkva. And I immediately went on to Orahovac. From Orahovac, I continued on towards Velika Hoca and arrived at my command post, that is, the feature of Krasta [phoen], overlooking Velika Hoca. You can see it on this map. By virtue of my decision, Bijela Crkva was not encompassed by the blockade, because it was my estimate that there were no terrorists in Bijela Crkva. That means that there were no terrorists from Bijela Crkva but they were in other locations. This can also be seen on this map. In Bijela Crkva, there was a standing police post. There was one in Zrze village, and near Bijela Crkva there was a police checkpoint, so you could safely reach Bijela Crkva and travel on. Police units that had come a bit earlier had already passed through Bijela Crkva. When I was passing through, it was completely quiet. The population was probably still there. You could only hear the dogs barking because the army was passing through the village, but the army was not passing through in combat columns. It was passing through in its vehicles. In the Bijela Crkva village itself, not a single bullet was fired at the army and there was no need for the army to return fire, and the army marched through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, is Bijela Crkva on the map which is on the board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. It is on the big map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what's the purpose of referring to this other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the so-called decision map. It was created two years prior to the operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the one that matters for -- for our purpose of investigating what happened, isn't it? We can see from it that Bijela Crkva was not included in the -- in the areas which you required to be examined.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Correct. That's precisely what I'm saying. And you can see this on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is really distracting me. I'm trying to fit it into the overall pattern, and I think the other map is a better one to refer to. What is the exhibit number of the map which is on the board? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you. It's 360. And Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that is a detailed map, a detailed section of the map of a larger scale than the map itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. The map on the board is 359.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 359. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, 358. And the map on the ELMO is 360.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This commission, this team of experts, was in possession of this map but this map shows the entire operation and all the activities. This map here is of a larger scale, and they wanted us to show the activities of the unit on this smaller map. The decision map shows how it was designed to conduct the operation, and this larger scale section was demanded so that we show how the operation actually happened, at various hours, ending with 1800 hours. So you can use these two maps to compare what the plan was with the actual operation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This other microphone switched itself off. I hope it can be turned back on. Yes, it's turned on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you have just explained - and that is also recorded in your statement given to the Commission for Cooperation with the ICTY - that the army passed through in a marching column and there was no fighting. In the second of two paragraphs, you say that you, having received this assignment, asked for information again and you were informed again that there were no problems in this village, that they passed through peacefully and there was no fighting. So from all this knowledge -- and we are talking about your unit.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What it says here in the indictment; namely, that "On or about 25th of March, 1999 forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded and attacked the village of Bijela Crkva"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not correct. Bijela Crkva was never surrounded or attacked, as you can see from this map. My unit was there only on the 25th. After that, it continued operations along other axes. I continued passing through Bijela Crkva after the 25th of March up to the 4th of April. I passed through Bijela Crkva when I travelled to Orahovac and later on towards Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any changes in the situation on those days in Bijela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can say, there was nothing. Just as on the first day, I passed through quite normally. I didn't notice anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Who is Colonel Vlatko Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vlatko Vukovic is my commander, commander of the 2nd Motorised Battalion from Djakovica. He was in command of Command Group 2, the one that is marked in these two places on the map. That is the only combat group out of my brigade that passed through these populated areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We also have his statement in tab 362. That is therefore a statement made by the unit commander from the same force that passed through this village.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All combat group commanders, up to Combat Group 7, were required to give statements and in the course of two months in 2002 they did give statements. As far as Vukovic is concerned, because Bijela Crkva and Celine were along his axis, his company commanders were asked to give statements too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says here in the penultimate paragraph of his statement: "There was no search conducted in Bijela Crkva village. He was informed that in Mirna village -- he was informed that the village was quiet and the forward security had been deployed to the east of the road coming out of the village. Combat Group 2 vehicles passed through the village from 500 hours to 0530 hours."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in accordance with our estimate. Our estimate was that there was going to be no resistance put up against the army and that we would be able to pass peacefully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask these exhibits to be admitted too, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course an entirely new issue arises for your consideration because it's clear, although it got obscured along the way, that the map, 360, and the statements, 361 and 362, are not material produced in the course of a contemporaneous inquiry of the kind we were looking for, for example, with Racak and never found. Were prepared specifically in respect of inquiries in the allegations into this indictment. They are material we haven't seen before today -- I mean, subject to the day or so we've had sight of them in advance -- and I have yet to be able to establish whether they are -- they would constitute material that we should have received as responsive to our RFAs. I'll -- it will take some time to tie that down, and I'm in the middle of trying to do it at the moment. In all probability, the breadth of the request for assistance being what they were, this is material that should have been provided to us by the authorities, and the suggestion that either the commission or the National Council were here to provide material to us is one that's a characterisation about which we have to be very careful. Now, material produced for the purpose of this litigation is material that under the Chamber's own rulings is material that may not be admitted and certainly not necessarily for the truth of its content. So that when we look at, for example, not only the witness's own statement but also the statement of the other officer concerned, this is an attempt to produce significant evidence by hearsay when it was actually specifically prepared for the purposes of these cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's only the one document, Mr. Nice. 360 the witness was given and used, and is here to speak about, and it relates to the -- the other one, 358. 361 is his own statement and he's here to adopt -- he has adopted it. So it's neither here nor there. There may be a issue between you and -- and Serbia about the disclosure, but that wouldn't affect the issue, as far as I'm concerned, with the witness here. But 362 falls into a completely different category.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just dealing with the first two points, I'm not sure -- I tried to look up both passages of questioning about the map 360, and I'm not sure whether it is merely a copy of an earlier map or whether it is actually a re-drawing of a map in detail, and I suspect it's the latter and not the former. So far as his own statement is concerned, statements made for the purposes of litigation in these trials can indeed be produced when they're produced by 92 bis or 89(F). And the fact that these statements existed and weren't served until these exhibits were served on us is yet another matter of regret when considered beside the proposition that all this material should have been dealt with in advance by documents that could have set out the witness's position. Your Honour is quite right as to 362; it falls into an entirely different category -- not an entirely different category. It has a different potential danger about it in that it's relied on the truth, it comes from a witness, prepared for the litigation, and the witness isn't going to be here. I'm not -- my policy throughout has not been to be particularly restrictive because I know that the Chamber is -- or at least I always assumed that the Chamber wanted to be inclusive rather than exclusive. But it does seem to me here we've met a category of material about which the Chamber may wish to make different decisions from the normal course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Kay, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I keep on forgetting. It's because the table has been moved. On the issues expressed by His Honour Judge Bonomy concerning the matters up to 362, those documents, I don't think those create a particular problem in terms of admissibility in relation to the map and indeed his own brief statement. Let's -- let's look at the realities of this. This is a -- a very brief explanation that was given to some sort of commission in relation to the indictment. Perhaps we ought to hear a little bit more about the -- the commission. 362 does fall into a -- a different category, but we have to know whether the Prosecution is objecting or not to its admission, and it seemed to me on the one hand Mr. Nice was raising a matter but not actually going for the full hog of an -- an objection. And to clear the decks, let's find out whether they want it in or not. There may be reasons why they want this material in, looking at it myself. But let's be explicit about it and not waste time taking points, if -- if that can be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's 362?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, my objection is -- my observations about the first two documents remain. But as to 362, I haven't yet had an opportunity fully to investigate it or to consider it in relation to the answers of this witness. Now, the Chamber's moved to the position where it wishes - and I understand this - for good order to deal with admissibility as documents are produced. At an earlier stage we from time to time dealt with documents on the basis of marking them for identification and dealing with them conclusively at the end. I don't want to exclude a document that I might then find their value in for the purposes of cross-examination when all this material is analysed before cross-examination starts more fully. And it may be that the appropriate course is to mark it for identification. But if you want to know whether I object to it, do I object to it for the truth of its content, absolutely, yes, I do. Because this is a hearsay statement of a significant kind and it's produced for the purposes of this litigation and it hasn't been served properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what's the point of marking it for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, because if -- if -- well, I suppose if we mark it for identification for and I choose to cross-examine on it because there's material of benefit in it for the Prosecution, or interest to the Prosecution, then at least I'm not, as it were, being inconsistent. If I had it excluded and then want to bring it back for the purposes of cross-examination, it might be thought to be a bit add. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are actually a number of them. It's just one of a series of five or six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's 372 or 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So even more in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. So that I certainly object to the production of this material for the truth of its content. But that's my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit the witness's statement -- we'll admit the witness's statement 361. That's his statement. He has adopted it. As well as his map 360. And the other statements produced for the purposes of this -- of the proceedings, 362. And we are trying to determine how far that goes to. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems to go to the end of this binder, 395 -- 394. And I notice that 381 is this witness's report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for each and every one of these events -- may I proceed now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that this was done for the purpose of this Court and directly for this Court. This is what the expert team requested from us. The General Staff commission for cooperating with the Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. There are several tabs here that pertain to one specific event. Then there is yet another event. For each and every one of them, there is a statement of mine or of my officers who were in that direction or at that particular location. So practically there are several maps here and along with each map there is a statement of mine. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there anything in what the witness is saying? That -- he's making the -- a nice point that they were not prepared for the purposes of ICTY proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was checking this through because I had to go back to remind myself what was -- what was said. The commission sent these documents to Mr. Nice's office, as -- as was his evidence, and it was for cooperation with the Prosecution, if one looks at the terms of -- of his evidence. So it wasn't actually prepared for the Defence. They were documents that were prepared for the Prosecution and the commission that was established for cooperation between Serbia and the ICTY. So we seem to have not an issue of failure of notice of the Prosecution with these particular documents. They've obviously had them for some considerable time and have been able to consider them. In this regard, the Defence is using materials that were prepared for the Prosecution. That's what's come about by -- by this, which is a -- a slightly different set of circumstances than we originally envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They were prepared for the purposes of ICTY proceedings, then they ought properly to have come through 92 bis or 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 89(F) would be -- given the terms of the evidence, it would be 89(F), as I don't think there's been any Defence evidence to which this would be cumulative testimony. It would be an 89(F) statement that would be required to produce it. I have to consider that. I -- Judge Bonomy looks quizzically at me at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If they were prepared for the Prosecutor's Office, I mean, that's for the purpose of -- of ICTY proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not these proceedings though. Not this litigation. And that's the definite -- that's the distinction I make, because as far as this accused is concerned, it's his litigation that is the point at issue in relation to the admissibility. This was -- this was produced in general terms for the assistance of the Prosecution, to cooperate with them. And it's quite clear that the commission of experts were -- were working on behalf of steps taken by the Prosecutor herself to encourage cooperation between the authorities in -- in Serbia and her own department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a very brief remark indeed. I'm sure that all of those watching this are aware of this. All this cooperation that the present-day authorities in Yugoslavia have with this place here pertains to cooperation with the other side, not with me. And the assistance that is rendered is rendered to the other side, not to me. Everybody knows that. I have had no assistance whatsoever. These are documents -- or, rather, statements of officers who were subordinated to General Delic. These are officers in his brigade, and they provided their own knowledge in detail as to what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? But in closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think you need to say -- you don't need to say anything else. We will be considering the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wanted to ask Mr. Nice: The point has been made that these documents must have been in your possession all through and indeed they're such that they must have been -- there would be an obligation to disclose them under Rule 68. What has happened in these regards?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The answer is at the moment I'm not in a position to give you a definitive answer one way or the other on whether we received all or any of this particular category of document. I'm certainly not aware that we have. But there are two other points that ought to be made: One is that simply to attach the word "cooperation" to a body or to a commission doesn't mean that that's what it does. And it -- that's important. It's not unimportant. Because the flow of material from the authorities to the Prosecutor's Office is on particular terms. Indeed, I was going to raise them with the witness and probably will in due course -- which don't typically involve the wholesale and surrender of material of this kind. The material comes in answer to particular requests. Now, having said that, there's another aspect of the history that the Court will learn about at some stage, and that is that this witness has indeed made a statement and to an extent cooperated with the Office of the Prosecutor in respect of activity of the KLA and material was provided in respect of that side of prosecution by or with his cooperation and assistance. Not necessarily through the commission. And so not untypically and not unusually you have a different -- potentially different response from either individuals or from bodies in respect of either KLA material or in respect of Serb-side material. Within the provision of that material, I'm not at the moment aware that we've received these documents. I am checking it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the answer to this though would be -- to follow the course you suggest, which gives you time then to explore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What has happened before a final decision is taken in relation to the documents and meanwhile the documents can be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can be looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, are you taking the position that on the basis that they're marked for identification that the accused can explore them with the witness? Because it becomes a rather sort of unreal exercise, doesn't it, if we do that and then we decide not to admit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not an unprecedented exercise because we've been looking at a lot of documents, the admissibility of which has been in issue. That's why I said at the beginning of this I'm don't -- I'm not disposed or wish to take a particular restrictive approach, but I do say that these documents, given that they were clearly prepared with this litigation in mind - and I'll say a sentence about that - would be under your present rulings, I think, inadmissible, for the truth of their content. And the sentence I want to add is that the witness said that -- and this is at page -- it reads as page 14 on the version I've got at the moment. It says: "When the Commission for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal summoned all the commanders and took from the indictment all the villages mentioned, not just on my territory but throughout Kosovo and Metohija, and they gave us such excerpts from maps like this one." So that he was clearly explaining at that stage that the exercise that was to generate this material was in fact related to this indictment on an itemised village-by-village basis. I can see the concern that His Honour Judge Bonomy has about the use of time that may be wasted, and the -- the accused could be invited to deal with these -- this category of documents in summary form because, of course, if in due course or in outline form -- if in due course they are admitted for any purpose, then the documents speak for themselves and the witness may have nothing much to add to them. If they're excluded, then they will be of no value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As for the map, my understanding is that the commission gave a clean map to the witness and it is the witness who marked -- who made the markings. Is it not the case? Is it right, Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In which case, again -- Your Honour is right. In which case then again the map of course similarly to the statements which were prepared for the purposes of commission is not an original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what would be the difference of 89(F)? The witness comes to the court and he testifies to the veracity of his statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely indeed. I means that's what I've said -- if you remember, what I said was this material simply makes it more regrettable that these processes weren't used when the material apparently was already in existence. It could have been served ages ago. It would have helped us all. But in a difficult area, I would respectfully go back to my position and the one tentatively raised as appropriate by His Honour Judge Bonomy but encourage brevity with the handling of the documents at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, as indicated earlier, we'll admit the witness's statement and his map; that's 360 and 361. And we propose to mark for identification the statements made to the Commission for Cooperation with the ICTY. Mr. Milosevic, we encourage you not to spend too much time on these statements. You should find a -- a summary way of dealing with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, please, could you just explain this to me: When you say that you were asked that all the events in Kosovo and Metohija should be clarified and then you used the word "indictment," does it pertain to this indictment or all the indictments that were issued against officials of the FRY in Yugoslavia and the army in relation to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It pertains to all indictments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all the questions that are raised in what Mr. Nice said were the subject of work of this commission. Did it understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we just have a correction in the transcript to that effect? It would not be a good thing to have what Mr. Nice said remain in the transcript, in view of the cooperation with the Tribunal that was sporadic and that it evolved out -- apart of this commission and the expert team. I have been cooperating with this Tribunal, the office in Belgrade, since 2002. That is a great many number of hours, over 3.000 hours of work for the Office of the Prosecution, and it went through the expert team. So every contact I had with the investigators of the Tribunal was in the presence of the members of the expert team as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Mr. Delic, you were given credit for your cooperation by Mr. Nice when he spoke. The point he is making was one about notification. It may all have happened as you say, but the question that's outstanding is how much of the material actually found its way to the Office of the Prosecutor. And because no notice was given until you were giving your evidence of these documents coming in, there hasn't been an opportunity to check that. And once it's been checked, the position will be resolved. And that's why we will mark these documents meanwhile for identification. It will be resolved in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basic problem is that in 2003 this entire team was dissolved on the basis of the decision of the Minister of Defence. The first decision Minister Tadic made when he assumed office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us proceed with the case. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, have I understood this correctly? Can I use these statements in putting questions to the witness, or can I not use them when putting questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may use them, but we have encouraged you to be -- to be brief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Major Janos Sel?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Janos Sel is a commander of a company in the 2nd Motorised Battalion?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the leader of the unit that specifically went through Bijela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, his unit went through Bijela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any other unit apart from his pass through Bijela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Other parts of the 2nd Motorised Battalion, the mortar platoon of 120 millimetres, and other units too, other platoons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All the units that went through, were they under the command of Colonel Vukovic, whose statement we saw a few moments ago, and was Colonel Vukovic under your command?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were no other troops there except for my units. They all belonged to the 2nd Motorised Battalion and they were under the command of Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So Major Janos Sel and Captain First Class Feta Elifat whose statement we have in tab 364, and Seargent First Class Oliver Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Ilijevski --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was platoon leader in that battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Captain Milovan Zivkovic. So all of them are officers serving on units that passed there.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Zivkovic was actually seconded only to that battalion. He did not belong there organically. He was sent there during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, but at the moment he was on the ground and that is the basis on which he gave his statement about what he knew.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All these statements up to tab 366, do they confirm what you said in relation to Bijela Crkva and your experience and your knowledge from that time? Because I noticed that they have a common denominator. They all say they were there, that they were there at the time, that nothing had happened, and that they heard about the alleged crimes in the book as seen, as told?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They speak of that only more specifically because they went through town in another direction. I moved along the asphalt road when I went to Orahovac. So they only speak more specifically about one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all the units that went through and all your knowledge from that time as well, because you said that later on all the way up to the first days of April you passed through Bijela Crkva and that there were no attacks on the village there, that there were no siege of the village or no such thing.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the way up to the 4th of April, I passed along the same road when I was on different assignments; that is to say, the asphalt road from Bijela Crkva to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were no traces whatsoever of fighting that might support the truth of the allegation in the indictment that I read out.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from the map, there were no combat operations whatsoever in Bijela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From these documents and from your personal knowledge of events, do you come to the same conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. So what it says here, that they surrounded and attacked the village of Bijela Crkva, you and your commanders say that this is not true.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely untrue. Bijela Crkva was never encircled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The indictment goes on. I won't mention the paragraph number again because it's in the same paragraph. It says that "Many villagers from Bijela Crkva fled along the river to Bijelo Selo and that they were forced to hide under the railway bridge and coming closer to the bridge, the forces of the FRY and Serbia opened fire on a number of villagers, killing 12 persons, including 10 women and children." Do you know anything about this and can you comment on what the indictment states about Bijela Crkva? Are you familiar with any of these events?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of any of this. I only heard about it in connection with the indictment. It says here: "They fled along the Belaja River. This is illogical. This small river does flow through Suva Reka but along the Belaja River that would mean that they were fleeing north, towards Orahovac and the shrubs and woods there. If anyone felt the need to flee, as far as I can see, nobody did, it says here "Belaja River" and then there's mention of a bridge. I'm very familiar with this territory. It is a plain which -- on which there is farmland and only vegetables are grown there. There are no shrubs there or anything of the sort, only vegetables, so that this in fact is one of the most fertile territories in Kosovo and Metohija. So if anybody wanted to flee, it would not be logical to flee out into the open; it would be more logical to flee in the other direction, where there were shrubs. So it's simply illogical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to what you and your subordinate commanders say and the members of your unit, there were no combat operations. So was there any fleeing? Did you observe anybody fleeing the village? Or did any of your officers observe anybody fleeing?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the statements made by my officers - and I have spoken to them - we were there. We passed through the village. The village was completely quiet. On the other side of the village, we went towards the Amovac feature and then the village remained behind us. We did not see anybody fleeing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... clarify this, General. You were actually in Bijela Crkva on the 25th of March with your men. You went through.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And there was no incident there, no fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No fighting. No incident. The troops passed through not in combat formation but in a marching column. It stopped on the other side of Bijela Crkva after having passed through, and then it spread out facing the Amovac feature and the villages of Celine, Nogovac, and Brestovac, where we had reliable information that the terrorist forces were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But do you recall the date of the 25th of March specifically as being the day when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recall everything I did on that day and all my activities later on. I did not linger in Bijela Crkva. I saw that my unit had arrived on time and had already left Bijela Crkva and that they were in their positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I asked that because the indictment is not specific as to the date. It says "on or about the 25th of March, 1999."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you about all those days while my unit was in that area, ending on the 28th of March. After that date, my unit was in the broader area but further away from the village of Bijela Crkva. The units that passed through Bijela Crkva did not return through Bijela Crkva. There -- the time they spent in Bijela Crkva was the amount of time they needed to pass through on trucks, several minutes, that is. On the other side of Bijela Crkva, they spent between half an hour and an hour there, until the beginning of the fighting, and then they proceeded towards the villages of Celine and Nogovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You don't allow, then, for the possibility that forces of the FRY and Serbia might have gone through Bijela Crkva a day or two before the 25th or a day or two after the 25th of March and the incidents might have taken place as set out in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The units could certainly not have passed through earlier. And I guarantee that my units never passed through Bijela Crkva again after that. In the month of May, which was about two months later, there was fighting in Bijela Crkva, but my unit did not participate in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just raise a matter for you? Because it's obviously of interest to Your Honour and it's pertinent to the indictment. The evidence called by the Prosecution on this matter related to that date of the 25th of March, Isut Zhuniqi was the witness on the 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Popaj and Jemini.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it's clear we are talking about the 25th. Mr. Milosevic, I think we'll just take the break now. It's time for the break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're still dealing with Bijela Crkva, count 66(b) -- or rather, paragraph 66(b) of the indictment. Apart from what I've already quoted, it alleges the killing of 12 persons and goes on to say: "The forces of the FRY and Serbia then ordered the remaining villagers out of the stream-bed, at which time the men and older boys were separated from the elderly men, women, and small children. The forces of the FRY and Serbia ordered the men and older boys to strip and then systematically robbed them of all valuables. The women and children were then ordered to leave towards an adjacent village called Zrze. A doctor from Bijela Crkva attempted to speak with a commander of the attacking forces, but he was shot and killed, as was his nephew. The remaining men and older boys were then ordered back into the stream-bed. After they complied, the forces of the FRY and Serbia opened fire on these men and older boys, killing approximately 65 Kosovo Albanians."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the number, Mr. Robinson, you asked me to give you a reference for. It's here. "A number of men and older boys survived this incident and other persons hiding in the vicinity also witnessed this incident. In addition, forces of the FRY and Serbia also killed six men found hiding in an irrigation ditch in the vicinity. These persons killed, who are known by name, are set forth in Schedule B."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you say about these allegations, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th, with regard to army and police units, something like this could not have happened. Up to 1200 hours my units were not in Bijela Crkva but in the direction of Celine. My subordinate commander and other subordinate commanders would have informed me had something like this happened. As regards the units under any command, it's absolutely impossible for anyone of my officers to have done that without my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, Mr. Nice's witness Isut Zhuniqi from Bijela Crkva testified that 16 policemen opened fire on 13 Kosovo Albanians, civilians, who were between the bridge and the police about 50 metres away from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, he testified on the 6th of June, 1992, [as interpreted] and the transcript page is on 6442 and 6443. I will read out a part of the transcript to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says here, among other things -- the transcript is in English: "[In English] Some 700 villagers gathered in the stream and the witness and his family walked for about a kilometre in the direction of Rogovo." [Interpretation] Then he goes on to explain, this representative of Mr. Nice, that he showed it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Little matters, but the language is becoming quite carefully slanted at achieving an objective. He's not a representative of mine. He's a witness I called. The accused knows that, and it's different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Mr. Milosevic, you -- you may consider whether it's necessary to delve more into Bijela Crkva. I mean, the witness's evidence is a clear and unmitigated contradiction of the allegation in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... then the -- what is in the indictment is not -- is not substantiated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we are now dealing with testimony which has been copied into the indictment. And when I say "the representative of Mr. Nice," I say this because he's speaking in the third person singular. Mr. Nice's representative was quoting from the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... any comment on that. He's not a representative of Mr. Nice. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they walked for a kilometre in the direction of Rogovo. And then he says: "[In English] Minds [Previous translation continues] ... taking cover because appeared to be sniper firing in their general direction." [Interpretation] Do you have any knowledge of snipers shooting at those people in that area, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at this map, here you will see where part of my unit was the whole time, which was in the blockade, and their one and only task was to prevent a possible breakthrough of the terrorists towards Drim and the Albanian border. The officer -- any officer who was there would certainly have observed anything going on in the area because it's only a kilometre or less than a kilometre away from him. As I was practically born in the area, I passed along this route thousands of times. I'm telling you this is a very flat area, a plain, with hardly any trees on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it. The soil is used to grow only vegetables, peppers, tomatoes, watermelons and so on. If we're speaking of 600 men --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He mentioned 700.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even 50 people could hide there, let alone 700. That's a huge mass of people. It's completely impossible. If you look at the map, even someone who knows nothing of topography can see that this is a plain. As far as the River Drina, it's completely flat. Anyone moving in any direction on that plain would have been observed either from the road or from the areas of Bijela Crkva or Celine or the asphalt road near Drim. My officers who were here or the officers who were in the Celine area would have reported on everything that happened on the 25th, regardless of whether it was my forces or the MUP forces that were affected. Had I -- in other words, I never received any information to this effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same witness says: "About 9.30, they were observed coming along the same direction [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] There had come a squad of some 16 policemen dressed in camouflage wearing armbands. They were all armed with AK-47 assault rifles and had foot-long knives in scabbards attached to their belts." [Interpretation] And later he says that he saw 13 Kosovo Albanians who had still not reached the bridge but they were in front of them. The police was close by, and the police shot at them and only one two-year-old child survived. Can you comment?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. All this reference is to knifes, the police was in their normal police uniforms carrying their establishment weapons. The only kind of police I saw were such policemen. I don't know what it means, "armed with long knives." The police have automatic rifles and they have knives, ordinary knives that serve for cutting barbed wire and similar activities. They are part of the combat set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these AK-47 rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are domestically produced rifles, a model similar to Kalashnikov 47, but it is domestically produced in the Crna Zastava factory in Kragujevac. It is part of the establishment weaponry of both the army and the police. It is the same system as Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did they have camouflage-style uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police did have their own kind of camouflage uniforms that were somewhat different from those of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he says that 65 people were killed, as I have read from the indictment. You have already commented on that. He later goes on to say that he had found cover. And on page 6444 he says he found 40 or some more villagers from Bijela Crkva also in hiding who informed him that the entire village can be destroyed with only some two houses not burnt down. Can you comment?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a blatant lie. I have already said there was no action, no operation in Bijela Crkva because there was no need to conduct any. The village was completely quiet and peaceful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then he says that he was on his way to visit his family in Zrze on the 31st of March, and later he went to Nogovac. That's on page 6445.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you, General, giving positive evidence that on all occasions when you went through the village there was no sign of any property having been burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That evidence is in my statement. Precisely on the 25th of March in the evening in Velika Krusa I saw that some houses were destroyed and there had been action obviously against these houses. That is written in one of my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, General, we are talking about Bijela Crkva now.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bijela Crkva, there was absolutely no operation whatsoever and there was no destruction in Bijela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, would you exclude a possibility of a -- paramilitaries, whether illegal or legal, paramilitaries could have perpetrated these kind of crimes after police and army had passed by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are discussing the 25th here, and I can testify to the entire period up to the 4th of April, which was the last time I passed through Bijela Crkva. Bijela Crkva as a village was completely fine. After that, I passed through only once more, in May. And as for the paramilitaries: In my own zone, I did not suffer and I did not allow any paramilitaries. They were regular police units and regular army units. This was an inter-ethnic conflict, and every inter-ethnic conflict is foul. What I don't exclude is that in some parts of my territory during the curfew and during the bombing something might have happened. But as for Bijela Crkva, this allegation that it was burnt down, destroyed, is absolutely not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can I take it that that never happened at any stage, that the village survived and survives to this day, intact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can talk only about what I saw myself. Up to the 4th of April, I passed through Bijela Crkva every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you saying you know nothing about its fate after the 4th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have said that I passed through Bijela Crkva once more, in the month of May, going from Orahovac. And at that time, Bijela Crkva was in absolutely the same condition as before the 25th of March. After that, there were other units located there, but I know that there was fighting on several occasions in the area of Celine, in the area of Pirane, and I'm not quite so certain but I think there were no operations around Bijela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you were dealing with the commission, which I think was 2003, did you go to the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After 1999 and the 14th of June, when I left the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, it was impossible for me to return there, even if I had wanted to, because my property remains there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said that there's an operation in Celine. Could gunshots or shellings, the sound of them could be heard in Bijela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are two neighbouring villages only several hundred metres away. If you look at the map, you will see that. This map does not even reflect the current situation because many new houses were built in the meantime. These houses are very close by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's true that tanks passed by Bijela Crkva and the -- the inhabitants of Bijela Crkva might have heard some gunshots and shellings, sounds of fighting in all the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But they could have noticed that the army had passed through their village and that there had been no activities in their village and the army had moved away, and throughout the day they could have heard operations growing more and more remote from their village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this witness says that he went to Nogovac on foot, found shelter in a barn -- [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... When a low-flying plane bombed it or bombed the area, causing the roof to collapse." [Interpretation] And then he says --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we have the page number. Although thus far I've found difficulty in tying up the page numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall I give you in electronic form?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you've got them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's 6438, line 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6445, transcript page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you say about this low-flying plane that bombed Nogovac? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which day was it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says here it was on the 31st of March when he went to Nogovac. He says: "There were many people there whom the Serbs ordered to gather in one place, that he himself was in a barn when a low-flying plane bombed the barn, or that area, as he put it.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The witness is probably talking about the 31st. The bombing happened in the night of the 1st, but it was the NATO aviation that bombed the village. And on the 26th, NATO bombed my unit, which was in the area of Opterusa. On the 26th with four aircraft and in the night of the 1st, there was a bombing of Nogovac but by the NATO, and I believe the Prizren Television made a film of the on-site investigation by the police. It was absolutely impossible for our planes to fly at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will no longer dwell on this witness, Isut Zhuniqi. But in any case, if I've understood you correctly, all that I've read out is not correct. The video even shows the US rocket that hit the houses in Nogovac, and you can see the destroyed village of Nogovac after the strikes by NATO aircraft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
