utterances.text: Thank you, General. We will now move to Celine village. Among these documents in tab 367 we have a map. Celine is, again, a village in Orahovac municipality. And I would kindly ask you to help us see what the army did in Celine. What can we see on this map in tab 367? The map is in the same format as the map you provided for Bijela Crkva.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We see the deployment of blockading forces of the army. We can see also the disposition of army units in Celine -- or rather, behind Celine at 1200 hours, and the deployment of army units at 1800 hours on that day, the 25th of March. We see the deployment of MUP units. And here we see the MUP unit that remained behind and continued to secure the Prizren-Djakovica road in the area of Mala and Velika Krusa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can we see on the map that the army had passed through Celine or by Celine, moving further on towards the east?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, the army was moving towards Retimlje, which is east, north-east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me now read out to you what is written in paragraph 63(A). 63(A), that regards my next question. It is part of the indictment related to alleged deportation. It says: "Orahovac column. In the morning of 25th March, 1999" -- so it deals specifically with the 25th of March. It doesn't say "on or around"; it says "on the morning of the 25th of March, 1999" -- "forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded the village of Celine with tanks and armoured vehicles. After shelling the village, forces of the FRY and Serbia entered the village and systematically looted and pillaged everything of value from the houses, set houses and shops on fire, and destroyed the old mosque. Most of the Kosovo Albanian villagers had fled to a nearby forest before the army and police arrived. On the 28th of March, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia forced the thousands of people hiding in the forest to come out. After marching the civilians to a nearby village, the men were separated from the women and were beaten, robbed, and all of their identity documents were taken from them. The men were then marched to Prizren and eventually forced to go to Albania." I have read out to you this entire paragraph, 63(A). Further below, there are references to Nogovac, et cetera, but we will dwell a bit on 63(A).

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting in Celine. Even according to our estimate, Celine village was covered by the system of defence of the terrorist forces. It had been active many times before and many times after throughout the war. Under combat, police forces entered the village and later my units came from the direction of Bijela Crkva. My units did not stop in Celine for any length of time. But what is written here about looting and pillaging and taking valuables from houses, that is simply unimaginable. How could I imagine my own soldier taking the liberty in the presence of his platoon commander, company commander, and superior officers, going into -- of going into houses and taking something? He would have been punished immediately. And what would he have done with anything that he took from a house? My soldiers came from the entire Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. They were not locals. It was the regular army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they wear? What did they carry?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They only carried their combat rucksack, containing one or two hand-grenades, 150 rounds regular ammunition, his own dry ration, the barest necessities. That's why it's called a combat rucksack. We usually conducted inspections of our troops after operations because it was prohibited in the strictest way even to drink water from local sources to avoid contamination or diseases. All they had was what they received from their units. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the forces came in, systematically looted and pillaged everything of value from the houses. What could, for instance, a soldier do with anything of any value? Where would he put it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. That happened absolutely never. It was not something done in the army. And in some cases, whenever a soldier took something from a civilian, he ended up court-martialled or disciplined by me personally. As far as forest is concerned --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here: "Most of the civilians ran to the nearby forest."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no forests in the area of Celine village. There is one here between Celine village and Nogovac village. It is what you -- what we call the Hoca River. In this territory, there are absolutely no forests. There is only shrubbery. That's this area. I've already said that up to Bijela Crkva and Celine there is a field, and here the terrain is slightly hilly, and afterwards come a great many vineyards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm just reminding you that I have read out a quotation to you. It says: "Thousands of people who were hiding in the forest, in the woods, that the FRY forces and the Serbian forces dealt with thousands of people hiding in the forest."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- an officer of mine told me that he found about 200 civilians near the brook between the villages of Celine and Nogovac. They came from both villages. It's not thousands. He didn't count them. But it was about 200 people, and that's what he wrote in his report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do? Did he force these 200 people to go somewhere, or what happened to them? What did he report to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that they were all supposed to go to where they came from. In his statement, he said that they should remain where they were until the army passed, and after that, those who were from Celine should return to their own village and those who were from Nogovac are in the immediate vicinity too. Later on the commander of my mortar battery, Feta Elifat, noticed that too, so they obeyed their battalion commander and they did indeed go to their own villages. However, it could not have been thousands at any rate; it was about 200 persons, civilians, primarily women, children, and elderly men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here "thousands," in the plural, but let it be 200. It says that "Men were separated from women, beaten up, and robbed, and that all their identity documents were taken from them, and that they were then marched to Prizren and eventually forced to go to Albania." I'm not talking about the number involved now. I'm talking about the allegations contained here, that they were treated in this way.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Treatment of civilians was clearly prescribed and regulated through several orders. All of those who violated these orders in any way were held accountable. So as far as this is concerned, I practically have nothing else to add. All civilians that were found were to wait for the army to pass by and then they would safely return to their own homes. The practice was that the army would not contact civilians, especially ordinary soldiers, that only officers should do that. No searches, no identification of civilians were carried out by the military if a police unit was nearby. That is police work, and they were allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, were there any occasions when any of your officers or men violated these orders and had to be held accountable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it did happen. It happened later, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in relation to this question put by Mr. Bonomy, what did this violation of orders consist of?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, it happened in the later period, when the border towards Albania was closed, because within the preparations for defending the country we laid mines five kilometres in the border belt, and even the road leading to Albania was mined. For a few days civilians could not go to Albania because they were not taken in by the Albanian side either, so there was this long column of civilians standing on the road for days. They didn't dare go off the road because everything had been mined. Soldiers had to stand next to them so that they would not have to keep saying that there were mines by the road all the time. A certain number of soldiers took money from the civilians then and they were arrested and court-martialled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any cases of any of your soldiers killing any civilians?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have had such cases too. I know practically of each and every specific case of this kind. They did not occur in this area here. They occurred later. My unit killed eight civilians: One in 1998, that was manslaughter in Opolje; and several civilians were killed during the war. Out of that total number, one civilian was killed by one soldier and he was arrested subsequently. I think that's contained in the documentation here. He was taken before a court-martial. Two officers and two soldiers killed two civilians. They were arrested later. And I think that in 2002 or 2003 they were sentenced by the military court-martial. The total of their sentence was 35 years. There was yet another officer who when ambushed in a village opened fire. So there were both terrorists and civilians there, people who were fleeing. He killed three civilians. He did not hit the terrorists. He was arrested after the war three days after this happened, and I think that he was sentenced but to a term in the prison hospital because of his medical condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, General. But now that you're dealing with this, would something like that ever happen without measures being taken in accordance with the law towards the perpetrators later?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever we received this kind of information - and it came down, or rather, up the chain of command and others came along the security chain - we always reacted when receiving such information. The security organ, the military police company would arrest all perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they were all sent further on to the war court in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's go back to Celine. I quoted everything that you heard. You gave your own comment. In relation to Celine, there is a statement that you signed and it's dated the 18th of December, 2002. And it says: "What we know about the alleged crimes in the village of Celine. " The statement is submitted to the Commission for Cooperation, to this expert team. And then you refer to information made public in the indictment against the former president of the FRY, Slobodan Milosevic. And you say: "I first heard of crimes allegedly committed in the village of Celine on the 25th of March, 1999."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the essence of this statement of yours -- or rather, in paragraph 3 you say: "From my conversations with unit commanders, I learned that Combat Group 2 had gone through the village of Celine after it had been taken by MUP forces. The village was fought over but nothing unlawful took place. Later in the afternoon, the unit continued moving towards the village of Retimlje."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not stated here, but it says in another statement of mine, a comprehensive one, I was in the Celine in the evening -- or rather, I passed through Celine. The asphalt road is very close to the village of Celine. And I was in the village of Velika Hoca in the evening and in Nogovac and I passed by Brestovac to Velika Hoca. I was supposed to give the police some assistance there, and then I returned to Nogovac where a police armoured vehicle had turned over, and there was an officer who was trying to get this combat vehicle out. At that time, around 2000 hours, I was informed that my barracks had been bombed. Then I passed through the village of Celine, came out on the asphalt road, and that was probably about 2100 hours -- almost 2100 hours when I passed through the village of Celine and went to Prizren to see the barracks that had been bombed that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, is the action in Celine something you would normally write an analysis about afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, this is not a separate action. An analysis is written about every event. We saw the previous analysis that has to do with this entire terrain. So specifically it's not written about Celine only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So do we have the analysis that includes reference to this action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, of course. We've already gone through it. Let me just see the tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 359.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the witness is doing that and before we lose the point, he spoke of "this tab" that we are currently looking at, 368, being a shorter version of a more comprehensive document. I'm sure it will help us all if we know if the comprehensive document has already been looked at or if it's within the papers or is it elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is yet to come, later.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] When document 359 was placed before the witness - that is an analysis of the brigade operations - I said that it includes all the events that follow later in the other documents. So it pertains to operations of the 549th Motorised Brigade in destroying Siptar terrorist forces in the wider area of Retimlje and the deblockade of Suva Reka-Orahovac. That is the time from the 25th of March until the 29th of March. And that is written already in line 1. What I quoted a few moments ago, what the analysis pertains to, that is the combat operations of the brigade in destroying the Siptar terrorist forces and deblocking facilities. So this analysis pertains to all these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think I see the reference to 7 on page 3 in --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here already on page 2 it says: "During the first day, in Bijela Crkva, Brnjaca towards the village of Celine. Then Mala Hoca, then Velika Hoca-Brestovac-Osmanica and so on and so forth. So that is what is described. The entire work of the brigade is described during these few days between the 25th and 29th. It's all included in this analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Delic, you said the operation in Celine took place on the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would it be possible that on the next day, 26th of March, a group of people who looked like Arkan's men with long beards, with shaved heads could be seen there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Arkan's men are often mentioned. The Siptar terrorists mentioned them most of all so that they could intimidate their own population. I never saw them. I would not allow such men to be in my area of responsibility anyway. Quite simply, as for such persons with very short hair, very long hair, with knives, wearing beards, there were no such individuals in my zone. I'd never allow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, are you aware of the order of the Supreme Command not to allow any paramilitary formations and if any such people were to be seen, they were supposed to be disarmed and arrested?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that, and all officers were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in document 369 there is a statement of Colonel Vukovic, whose unit was precisely in that area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the unit that passed through Bijela Crkva, through Celine, Nogovac, went by Velika Krusa. So they were moving along the west-east axis and towards Randubrava. That is where they were operating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to that -- or, rather, what we commented upon a few moments ago, in the fifth paragraph of this statement of his, he says that "At about 1400 hours he came across a group of civilians with some women, children, and elderly males among them. The group was hiding in the Hocanska Reka river-bed. There were about 200 civilians in the group. I spoke with an elderly man, and he told me they were from the villages of Celine and Nogovac. I ordered them to remain there until the soldiers had gone and then to go back to their villages. I know that the group of civilians went to the village of Celine later because I was informed about it by the commander of the fire support group, Captain Feta Elifat. I relocated the fire support group to the sector of Brinje. We did not go back to the village of Celine and I do not know what happened to this group of civilians." So that's what you knew too.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the valley of Hocanska Reka or the Hocanska Reka river-bed. It's a tiny little river, a brook. And there are very small Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. shrubs around it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says that the unit did not commit any crimes in the village of Celine or its surroundings and that he was not aware of some other unit having committed the alleged crime.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was constantly in contact with that commander, as I was with the commanders of the other combat groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the most part, this is a response to what is alleged in the book "As Seen, As Told."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before that book was published, in the year 2000, when the corps commander summoned all the brigade commanders, he provided us with some excerpts. He said Bijela Crkva, Velika Krusa and so on, that's up to you to say what happened there, so that in the year 2000 the commander asked for explanations and brief statements. Those statements were about a page long. Later on in this book published by the humanitarian right fund of Natasa Kandic "As Seen, As Told," we read a lot of details which resembled the allegations in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, who is Captain First Class Feta Elifat?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my 2nd Battalion, he was the commander of the 125-millimetre mortar battery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His statement is in tab 370, and it says: "In the village of Celine, I did not open fire because there was no request."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Celine was taken by the police units. If you look at the map, here is Bijela Crkva and here is the village of Celine. The mortar battery had taken up positions near Bijela Crkva, and the police were deployed from this main road in the direction of Celine. When the army arrived, Celine was practically already taken and fighting continued onward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if you remember, although I quoted extensively, it says: "On the 25th of March, the forces from the FRY and Serbia surrounded Celine with tanks and armoured vehicles." "Tanks" refers to the army. It says here that: "After shelling the village, they entered the village and then" -- is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is simply not correct. The term "to surround" means to encircle the entire village from all sides. And on each one of these maps, you can see that the police arrived from the south-west and that the army arrived from the west, in the west-east direction. The village was not surrounded at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says here that you first surrounded it, then shelled it, and then went to burn, loot, and so on.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is absolutely contrary to any kind of military logic. If you surround a small village, you cannot shell it, because if you did, you would have losses among your own men from your own fire. So it would be completely illogical, and I know such things did not happen there. I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Delic, in this tab, 370, which is a statement of Captain First Class of Feta Elifat, there's a passage which says that their observation post was at TT440. If you could tell me what that 440 is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a trig point. It's a term from topography. A trig point - I could find it on the map - means that it's an elevation. It's an elevation on the terrain and it's usually put on -- or if you want to observe, you usually do that on top of a hill. "TT" stands for "trig point" and it's a term from topography.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it possible when the commanders communicate each other through radio they identify themselves with the numbers, such as 444, "commander 444"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They all have code names, so they all have a name. My name was "Poljanica" for example. After that, I had a number, so that whoever was listening to me would know it was me. For example, I was "Poljanica 319." All my commanders were also "Poljanica" but they had other numbers. Each had his own number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does Commander 444 ring a bell to you? Is it possible that it is one of the code names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. The situation was similar in the police units. They had to have a name, a code name of some sort. I've told you what mine was. And that would be followed by a number. The number would designate the unit or the officer in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just on the trig point. If Your Honour looks at the map, just to the right of the block.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in connection with this area of Celine, in tab 371 there is a statement made by Warrant Officer First Class Oliver Ilijevski, and he says here that: "In the period from the 25th to the 28th of March, 1999 my rifle platoon took part in the blockade." He was a platoon leader?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a platoon leader from the 2nd Motorised Battalion from the 2nd Company of the 2nd Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. He says: "I took part in the blockade and search of the terrain and the destruction of STS along the following axis: The village of Bijela Crkva, the village of Celine, the village of Randubrava, the village of Donje Ratinje, the village of Neprebiste, this whole axis."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he passed along this whole axis mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he says: "After the march on the 25th of March, 1999 at about 0600 hours we took the line of blockade on the road near trig point 440 south-east of the village of Bijela Crkva about one kilometre towards the village of Celine. To my left was the platoon of Lieutenant Zivkovic, and to my right were parts of the special police unit detachment. At about 0730 hours my platoon came under fire from the village of Celine. We returned fire." And then he says that fighting lasted for about 40 minutes. And then: "The police entered the village and searched it. I presume that the routed STS retreated in haste towards the village of Randubrava and that the local population had withdrawn towards this village after the combat operations started. I went around the edge of the village and did not see any civilians. I then took a position on the Brdo sector" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he, too, says here that there were no civilians there and that he read about what is mentioned in the book "As Seen, As Told," that he read details about it but that he did not see this and that no other unit could have done this.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the platoon that passed along this axis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, what was the role of Natasa Kandic in relation to the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She is at the head of this fund for humanitarian -- human rights fund.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Humanitarian Law Fund. Interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I referred to her yesterday because in her book she also quoted the OSCE sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this is a book which she wrote that's being referred to here, not the OSCE book, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a book published by the Humanitarian Law Fund. Natasa Kandic is the head of this fund.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the book "As Seen, As Told"?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is book lists all the municipalities in Kosovo and Metohija and what allegedly took place there from village to village. When you read the book, you can see that most of the sources used were Albanian. Only Albanian sources were used and also OSCE sources in some parts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I understand correctly, Mr. Robinson, that allegations -- or, rather, that it is said here that this is an OSCE book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is that said?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we -- we all know the book about the book "As seen, as told." At the moment I suspect we're only interested in what the witness's understanding of that book is and we can deal with the consequences of that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic. And you were to try to go through these tabs as concisely as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying, Mr. Robinson, to go through it as quickly as possible, but all this refers to the allegations made by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the witness of the other side, Reshit Salihi from Celine, said here -- it's from the 19th to the 22nd of April, 2002, and the transcript is page 3542. He comes from Celine and he said: "On the 24th of March, the Serb army was" -- it says elsewhere that they were wearing black uniforms, so this is not in the statement, "that they opened fire on houses and buildings, including the mosque in Celine, that on that occasion they set fire to houses, that the units of the Army of Yugoslavia on that day surrounded the village of Celine, shelled it, set it on fire, and then the Army of Yugoslavia entered the village and opened fire on houses and buildings. This is almost identical to what Mr. Nice says in paragraph 63(A), but this is a witness brought here called by Mr. Nice. What can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that this is absolutely untrue. A date is mentioned, the 24th of March. And as can be seen in all the documents and orders, on the 25th of March in the morning, that's when the operation started. As for black uniforms, only the special units of the KLA had black uniforms and their military police. In our army, there are no black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's say he was mistaken in the date. But is any of this true, as far as the events go?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You did say that. It corresponds to paragraph 63(A) of Mr. Nice. As you say that it does not tally with the truth, do you feel that this witness is lying?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This witness is not telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's an improper question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about the attack on the old mosque?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to houses of worship and religious buildings, they received special treatment because any firing on such buildings is banned. These buildings, however, do not enjoy the same protection if they are used as sniper nests or if fire is opened from them. I know about some other buildings in this area. I think the mosque in Neprebiste, in Retimlje, in Landovica and in Pirane, I have information about those, but I don't have any information that there was fire opened from this mosque or that anybody fired on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This witness says that the Serb forces ordered the men -- men to separate off from the women and children, that their valuables and documents were taken and burned. After that the men formed a line and were marched at gunpoint to Prizren, and that they stood at the checkpoint with their hands raised for six hours. Can you say anything about these allegations. That's page 3543 of the transcript in the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is, if you look at this map, this is where my units were in the blockade. My major, now lieutenant colonel, Radivoj Paravinja was here. I spoke to him personally when I was trying to find out about all this. This could not have happened, for somebody to be marched at gunpoint or to be made to stand for six hours at a checkpoint, because my troops were from this crossroads as far as the village of Landovica. That's where they were deployed. And that's several kilometres. This could not have happened in this area without my receiving a report about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This witness also says that on the 26th of March, at about 0700 or 0800 hours in the morning, a group of over 40 policemen arrived at the Pisjak forest where five to six thousand refugees were hiding and threatening them with weapons, stole their money, jewellery, and personal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documents. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pisjak forest -- as I said, on this territory, as far as the line you can see on the map here, up to the Orahovac-Velika Hoca-Suva Reka line, this whole area is devoid of any kind of forest where 6.000 people can hide. These are vineyards for the most part. From the Mala Krusa farm and Odrovino [phoen] of Orahovac and the privately owned vineyards from these villages, there are no forests here. There are various streams which have shrubs growing around them, and near Retimlje there is a very small wood. The forests go up from this line here, on Mount Milanovac. I was not able to find the term "pisjak" on the map. They call the forest pisjak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it says "pisjak."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On our maps, regardless of their scale, I was unable to find such a term or place name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, another witness called by Mr. Nice, Agim Zeqiri from Orahovac, said that: "A column of refugees comprised of about 4.000 people and that it was followed by the army and the police while on their way to Albania." Could you now explain. It's on pages 757-758 of the transcript. Were these people expelled towards Albania, as this witness says?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The allegation is that the army expelled and escorted somebody. Absolutely never did the army expel or escort anybody on their way to Albania. You cannot consider as escort the fact that there were soldiers standing along the asphalt road leading to the border. The soldiers had to stand there for several days until this area was sealed off by tape. The soldiers -- the troops had to stand along the road to prevent anybody stepping away from the road and into the minefield. So the troops were there to protect the civilian population, but the road section concerned is from the border up to Zur village and another village, which I believe is called Muradem. Those were the only places where you could see troops standing along the road. Here as well the troops were standing along the road. I was informed by a commander of mine that on the 27th certain groups of civilians passed through going from different directions and they took the asphalt road, travelling in groups of several vehicles, but nobody stopped them, because they just passed through along the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this quotation, it's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Another witness, Isuf Jemini from Celine says in his statement that "By radio communication" -- and here we see the figure mentioned by Mr. Kwon, code 444 -- "he heard the voice of a policeman from Celine saying that many people in Celine had been killed; whereas, another voice allegedly asked: Was it a larger massacre than in Racak? And the reply to that was, 'twice larger'." That's in the transcript page 8562 and 8563. We heard this testimony on the 24th of July, 2002. Could you tell me first about this word "massacre" in Racak. Who used that word with regard to Racak?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I heard it was from Mr. Walker. I believe he was the first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anybody on our side, in our army, among our police who used the word "massacre," talking about Racak or any other place in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard anybody describing operations in Racak as a massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it seem logical to you for our policemen to talk amongst themselves and to use the word "massacre" to describe events in Racak?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of any such thing. I believe that is impossible. The communications that exist in the police are both vertical and horizontal, and they're our superiors. Such communications is not possible. At the end of the day, I had communications both with my units, and I had two communications -- communication devices that were used by the MUP and I could follow their communications as well. The reason that I was able to follow their communications was that they sometimes needed assistance, and the only one who could decide that assistance be given to them was me. That is why I listened to communications effected using these hand-held radios among MUP troops; although, I primarily listened to communication between my commanders. But something of this kind is nothing like what you would expect from either the army or the MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you had two radio devices of the MUP that were constantly on. Did you ever hear a code 444?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have had to hear yourself or anybody who listened to this radio traffic any such conversation, if it ever took place?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My subordinate commanders were not able to follow this radio traffic. I was the only one who could. My subordinate commanders could only communicate with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This testimony says that the conversation was referring to the massacre in Celine and that according to this conversation the number of those killed was double that in Racak. Now, tell me, what do you know about the losses of the Siptar forces in Celine, where the fighting took place?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Celine, the fighting lasted for about 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what your commander says -- your subordinate commander says in this statement.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the police was the first to come in the village of Celine, I have no information about the losses on the terrorist side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you have any idea how many were killed there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that prior analysis, it was stated that our estimate for this entire area covered by the operations was 75 or 85.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was 85.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 85. So since we encountered organised resistance and since defences were put up in terms of engineering and certain routes were mined by the terrorists, we did not find a single wounded terrorist; we found blood-stains. In one place I even found a bloodied cap and remnants of a skull. But the terrorists who were wounded were obviously pulled back together with the terrorist units deeper into that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any case, would you have had to have known about anything that happened in Celine?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my units were directly along the road, and you can see on the map the situation was the same for several years back. Here you see the intersection where the railroad diverts from the road. My forces were along here. They were blocking forces. Their only assignment was to prevent any possible breakthrough by the opposite forces, by the enemy, towards the Drim River. All these units were commanded by Major Paravinja. If anything had happened here directly near the road, either he or some other commanding officer would have had to see it, be it something involving the army or the MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, General. Thank you. Now, my request, Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Time for the break. But you had a point?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with the exhibits. I am asking for them to be admitted, those that we have already dealt with, and we have reached tab 372, that is, 371 inclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. 367 and 368, admitted, his statements. The others are marked for identification. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in document 372 we have a map showing Landovica. We have also a witness statement here, a statement by a Prosecution witness, referring to Landovica. But first of all let me ask you: What did the army do in Landovica and what can you say about the map under tab 372, showing Landovica? In fact, we have two maps here, 26th of March at 0600 hours and the same date 1200 hours.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Landovica is situated close to the road Prizren-Zrze-Djakovica. It is very close to Prizren, just a couple of kilometres away from Dusanova [phoen] village. In this village -- or its immediate vicinity, rather, is my command post during the war, and several times during 1998 and 1999 my command post was occupied. This is the village. Two to three hundred metres above it are artillery positions. These positions were engineered during peacetime and positions were taken there several times during military drills. The village is about 200 to 300 metres away. There are also defended positions and shelters from my units, the reconnaissance company, and the communications company -- the signals company, rather. I'm saying this because very frequently at this time we were in the close vicinity of Landovica and we believed there could be no terrorists there simply because we were so close by. And when we were planning this activity, we excluded Landovica village from the operation precisely due to my own estimate and the estimate of my commanding officers that Landovica is two to three hundred metres away only and there could be no terrorists there. That is why we situated the line of blockade outside of that village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute. I'm afraid the -- the map we are looking at through the ELMO is different from what I have. Mine says it's dated 26th of April and does not have that markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's different -- 26th of March. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two maps. One is dated the 25th, showing the deployment of units on the 25th. And the second one is for the 26th. I have now placed on the ELMO the map showing deployment on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, Mr. Kwon, that there are two maps in this tab. One is for the 25th at 0600 hours and the second is for the 26th. It's 1200 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We do not have the first one, dated 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can you explain both these maps? You can place the first one on the ELMO and then the second one.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the viewpoint of events in Landovica village, both maps are usable because the events took place on the 26th. We had better keep here the map referring to the 26th. The only difference is that on this map we can see the deployment of units -- other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 380 has the map for 25th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I see. Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Maybe the first map was included in 380 by mistake or something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's probably been a mistake, because there's nothing in my tab 380 and both were placed in this tab 372. But the important thing is that you have both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please explain, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the map of the 26th. This map shows where Landovica is and it shows the positions of the artillery battery of 122 millimetres, one of its parts, that is. And also the 128-millimetre rocket launchers battery. Then it also shows in front where the blockade forces are, and it also shows here where the units are further up, where the operations are taking place on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The operations did not involve the village of Landovica.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The village of Landovica, according to my estimate and that of my superior officers, precisely because of this immediate proximity -- or how should I put this? The fact that every year several times we were in the immediate vicinity of this village, my command post here, that is underground, we thought that 200 or 300 metres away from our positions the terrorists would not be there, they would not be organised, and that's why we excluded this village from the blockade and it was not supposed to be searched, or quite simply, the army was not supposed to enter it at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You wrote a statement about what happened in Landovica on the 26th of March. The event relates to the 26th of March, that is. And it's on the 18th of December, 2002 that you wrote your statement. This statement of yours is contained in document 373. And here in paragraph 2 it says: "No fire was ever opened from the village. We did not have any problems with the local people. That is why the village was outside the blockade line. Soldiers were forbidden to enter Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the village without officers or buy any items from the shops on the territory, especially food. The order was occasionally breached, however, with or without the knowledge of junior officers. Later interviews with soldiers revealed that soldiers from Landovacko Brdo occasionally went down to the shops in Landovica village to buy cigarettes, juice, sweets," et cetera. Now, there is a description here of what happened on the 26th. What was this all about, actually? Can you tell us briefly? Or will you just quote what you have already written in your statement? It's all the same.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I know from my conversations with the unit, the commander of the Howitzer unit, and that is my knowledge from that period of time. Although security organs also carried out their own investigation, there were actually two soldiers who survived. One was wounded and the other one was not wounded. In the briefest possible terms, four soldiers from this unit, because they came beforehand as well, knew that there was a shop in the village. They went down into the village. They went to that shop. The shop was closed, which was unusual. What I knew, I wrote down in this statement. They broke into this shop. They used force to open the door, that is. They took a few small bags of potato chips and some juice from the shop and they set out to go back to the unit. Fire was opened at them from the surrounding houses. Three soldiers were wounded. The soldier who was the first one in the column was not wounded. So since he could not help them because shooting was coming from several houses, he practically ran to his unit to say what happened. They reacted from the units immediately. First the commander informed me that they had wounded or killed soldiers in the village. I immediately ordered that these soldiers had to be taken out of the village since they said that they could not get into the village now, that there was strong fire coming from the mosque and from several houses, and now even from the outskirts of the village. Then I ordered that a platoon which was on the reserve force move to the village straight away. I ordered the commander of this unit that was with the forces in the brigade to single out part of the forces, and I ordered Combat Group 1, which was closest, to set out a tank immediately and to give it to that group. As it says in my statement, the fighting went on until dark. As soon as fire opened and before the army came in, the population which was in the village went in two directions, and with them part of the terrorists too. One group went through these vineyards here towards Gornja Srbica, the village of Gornja Srbica. And the others went to the area of the village of Atmadja, across the asphalt road. When the units arrived, two soldiers were dead and one was wounded. Later, when speaking to this soldier, he actually said that they were all hit, all three of them, since gunfire was coming from the neighbouring houses, that the terrorists got out of the houses. These two soldiers were moaning because of their pain. The terrorists walked up to them and fired an entire clip into each -- into each one of them. The third soldier pretended to be dead. He just lay there. He was seriously wounded with several bullets. But the terrorists just walked up to him, took his rifle, and went back to the houses. So the fighting went on there until nightfall. The terrorists who were withdrawing during the fighting towards the village of Gornja Srbica were practically assisted by a group that was behind the back, the village of Atmadja. Fire was coming at this unit from the back, so forces had to be engaged in order to neutralise that group too. So on that day in that village two soldiers were killed and one was seriously wounded. Later on when the village was examined, it was established that near the shop the headquarters for that village were located with part of the weapons, communications devices, ammunition, these maps. Later on bunkers were found in the village near some houses. We hadn't noticed that before. And concrete pillars were used to fortify these bunkers, those that are usually used in vineyards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you described that in your statement, and we see in document 374 -- your statement was document 373. And in 374, we see the statement of Lieutenant Colonel Radivoj Paravinja, who was in charge of that unit, I assume.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The dead soldiers came from his unit. At that time, he had a different assignment but he received orders from me to come to assist this unit with part of his forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His statement matches what you said in your statement, the information that you have.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Generally speaking, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will you be calling any of these persons who gave statements to the commission for cooperation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can call them as witnesses. Some of them are on the witness list. It depends on the significance that is attached to these statements that they had already given, but some of them can certainly testify in far greater detail because General Delic commanded that entire unit. I assume it would be useful to hear the testimony of one of his commanding officers from his unit for the particular areas that they were in charge of so that the situation would be quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's always a good strategy to get witnesses who are close to the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, a witness was here for the other side, Halil Morina about Landovica. He spoke about this event that you have just described and we also have a statement of Lieutenant Colonel Paravinja about what happened there. I'm going to quote a particular page of the transcript for you. 892 is the transcript page. I'm just going to quote a few words and then from some other pages as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... give us the date. I find that our page numbers don't match and sometimes the date's an easier method to track the transcript down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, will you assist in that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 21st of February, 2002. That's when he testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think maybe 25th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I have written here is the 21st. But possibly you're right, Mr. Kwon. At any rate, it is page 892 of the transcript. I'm just going to quote a few things from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He says -- he mentions a jeep: "[In English] A military vehicle came a few minutes after the shelling and I was with my brother and his wife. He came with me and there was shelling going on and firing into the air." [Interpretation] Further on, on page 893: "[In English] I saw them when they were burning the village. They killed a gypsy. And when they came down, they killed Avdi Gashi, an Albanian. And a paralysed woman, they set fire to her in her own home." [Interpretation] And then there's a question: "[In English] How long did the troops stay in your village? Until 7.00. [Interpretation] On page 894 at the very beginning it says [In English]: "Then we went to see what was happening, what had happened in the neighbouring houses. Then I went to our home. We saw that it was burnt." [Interpretation] Later on, on page 894: "[In English] That late afternoon, early evening, did you notice the condition of the mosque? "No. It was on the next day that I noticed it. On the 27th." [Interpretation] Then he says on page 895: "First I went to the neighbouring house and [In English] there were 13 dead bodies lying on the floor. Then we went to search in other houses of the village to see if there was anyone left. We didn't find anyone. And then we returned back home. No, first we went to bury -- we went to search for our family. 39 members they were. We didn't find them. Until 11.00, we looked around in the fields, in the brook, everywhere. We didn't find them. They had left for Prizren." [Interpretation] And then he's asked again [In English]: "I want to be clear about the mosque. You told us you saw it the next day, the 27th. We're on the 27th. Was it at this time you saw the mosque or was it later? "I saw it on 27th, at 11.00. We came from the field and went back home. Then a group of soldiers came and examined the corpses, and three of them went to the mosque. They entered the mosque. They had white ribbons on their arms and they started to fire at the mosque, to shell it. In ten minutes, I heard the explosive, a blast, and the minaret fell." [Interpretation] Then he says: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... they got down out of the car. They entered the mosque, they placed the mine, and I heard the explosion, and then I saw it toppling down. Nothing else."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... cars, and there was a Zastava car. Before they shelled the mine, they came and examined the corpses. Then they shelled the mine. They came back and borrowed a private Zastava, on which they loaded the bodies of the dead people." [Interpretation] So you've heard this witness's statement. He says that the village was heavily shelled. He says that 13 dead people were found in a house. Not to repeat everything I've already quoted from this testimony, what can you say about this testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This witness says that he was in the village all the time. In the village, from the 26th, when the shooting started, and onwards there was no one there and no one could return to that village because my unit was still on the position that is depicted here. They did not allow anyone to return to the village without reporting to the commander of the unit before that. So this story that somebody could be strolling around the village all the time is totally incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In document 375, there is a criminal report of the military police -- or rather, it says here: "Authorised official of the military police in Prizren, the 27th of March, 1999, against Siptar terrorists unknown on the basis of the well-founded suspicion that the said persons committed the crime of terrorism from Article 125 of the Criminal Code of the FRY because on the 26th of March, 1999 around 1400 hours in the village of Landovica near Prizren they launched an attack against four soldiers," and then the names of the soldiers are given, "and they were killed."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this report was submitted to the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the regular way of proceeding in connection with such events?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When such events occurred, criminal reports were submitted against the perpetrators -- or rather, perpetrators unknown, because at that time we could not determine who had attacked those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in this event in Landovica you have precise information as to who the soldiers were who were killed and who was the wounded soldier. Do you have details of the KLA members who were killed who had attacked these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several of them. Six or seven. I'm not sure about the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your forces arrived there, I understand that the civilians had already left the village.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those civilians were in the village until fire was opened on the soldiers. After that, quite a lot of time elapsed before the units arrived and before the first aid arrived about half an hour ago [as interpreted]. The troops from the reserve and those who were supposed to help arrived about one and a half hours later. The civilian population had left, and some of the terrorists had probably also left, and later on they fired at the reinforcing unit in the back, from the rear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Tell us something about the Official Note provided in tab 376, bearing the date the 27th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an Official Note issued by an authorised official of the military police who drafted the criminal report. He interviewed the soldiers in this unit. He was probably unable to interview the wounded soldier. I don't know. But he interviewed the soldiers who had been with them, and he drew up this note to describe what had happened and what the soldiers had been doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these Official Notes, in your statement, in the statement of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your superior commander, the events described differ significantly from the description given by the witness Halil Morina here.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The witness spoke of shelling. As I have already explained, we considered the village of Landovica to be a friendly village in our immediate vicinity, and we were surprised when our soldiers got killed in that village. We contacted the villagers -- or rather, we had contacts with them. On more than one occasion, I had been in that village or its immediate vicinity when I was checking my command post, which was underground. On one occasion, I had contacts with the head man of the village because sometimes the children would damage the door and sometimes they would cut the electricity wires in that facility of mine, but there were no other problems, no special problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does he also say that the mosque was blown up, that explosives were placed there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque was hit in the minaret, the tower, and the rest of the damage occurred because of the firing on the minaret. The village of Landovica held a special position geographically. It was in a depression, in a small valley. And from the top of that mosque, you could have control over all the approaches to the village. So simply we could not come close to the soldiers until we had fired on the minaret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had the minaret been fired from?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The minaret had been fired from. Fire was opened on our soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We will now go on to speak of Retimlje. Let us first look at the map in tab 377, and this refers to Retimlje.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just draw your attention: In paragraph 63(B) here, Mr. Robinson, Donje Retimlje is mentioned. This reads as follows: "On the 25th of March, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded with tanks and various military vehicles this village. It was shelled. Several villagers were killed. After this, forces entered the house. The villagers were forced to leave and go to the neighbouring village. In the village of Landovica an old mosque was burnt and heavily damaged by forces of the SFRY and Serbia. Some of the Kosovo Albanians fleeing towards Serbia were killed or wounded by snipers. Forces of the FRY and Serbia then launched an offensive in the area of Srbica and shelled the villages of Donje Retimlje - that's the village we have on the map now - and Randubrava. It goes on to say how the Kosovo Albanians were forced from their homes and sent to the Albanian border. I won't read on because the rest is about Prizren and we'll deal with that later because the General's command was in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, was Retimlje a terrorist stronghold and were there fortified facilities in the village and around the village? Please point to the map and explain what this is about. It's the map in tab 377.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Retimlje was the centre of this territory held by the 124th KLA Brigade. In Retimlje, there was also the headquarters of the 124th Brigade. Their military hospital was there, and the other facilities they needed. Donje Retimlje, which is also referred to as Gornje and Randubrava were positions which were very well fortified from an engineering point of view. In front of Randubrava and Donje Retimlje, mines were laid out with a -- special mines and these had been handmade. More than one such mine had been laid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you precisely whether Retimlje was a terrorist stronghold.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was one of the strongest enemy -- or rather, terrorist strongholds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Retimlje and the surrounding area, were there fortified facilities?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The surroundings of both villages, Retimlje and Randubrava, were fortified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In connection with Retimlje, you wrote a statement about what you knew, and that's in document 37 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before we move on, to better understand this map, could you read out the comments marked on this map, please. There's a legend and there's some comments on the markings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The legend says: "Disposition of forces at 1200 hours." That's shown in yellow. Then it says: "Disposition of forces at 1800 hours." And this means forces in the blockade. So there are three different colours here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the comments written in -- with the markings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next to the markings are the names of the units. So these are not comments but simply the names of the units who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please now take a look at the statement you made to the Commission for Cooperation, 18th of December, 2002. It's a statement made by you, is it, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One can see your signature here. And it's information about the fighting in the village of Donje Retimlje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 379?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 379.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't have a translation of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a very brief statement. I think it can be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are quite a number of the forthcoming tabs that are not translated and it's going to be quite difficult to deal with them unless we do get translations by Monday or Tuesday at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, would you please read this out. It's very brief, the statement that you made.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of the statement it says: "Combat operation began on the 25th of March, 1999 in the area of Suva Reka-Orahovac-Velika Krusa with the following purpose: To establish control in that part of the territory, to secure that roads Suva Reka-Orahovac and Prizren-Djakovica be passable, and to crush and destroy the 124th Brigade of the KLA and other terrorist forces in the said area. "The target of attack was not the civilian population. The attack began from a circular base, circular axis. Not a single village was surrounded or attacked. Our forces reached Donje Retimlje on the 26th of March, 1999. The village was captured only on the 26th March around 1700 hours. The village was defended by significant forces of the 124th Brigade of the KLA from favourable positions outside of the village and inside the village itself. The surrounding area of the village was completely well defended in terms of engineering and on southern axes to the village targeted action mines, improvised mines, were detected. Artillery began to act on the trenches on the 26th of March. "At the time of artillery action, there was no civilian population because they had left their homes earlier. Upon the capturing of the village, apart from the equipment of the terrorists and the facilities they used in the village, to the best of my knowledge not a single inhabitant was found nor did we hear any information, any reports that civilian -- that there were civilian casualties in the village."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, on the 17th of December, 2002 you wrote a more extensive statement referring to the activities of the 549th Motorised Brigade from the 25th to the 28th. You did so at the request of the Commission for Cooperation. It's in tab 381. What can you say about this statement?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement was written for each day. There was a statement for each day of the operations, not for particular villages. I as a brigade commander wrote a statement for the entire operation and every commander of every combat group wrote a statement about his own troops. And there was a statement for each of these dates: The 25th, the 26th, the 27th, and the 28th. And along with each statement, there was a map of all the operations on that day representing the situation at 6.00 a.m., at 1200 hours, and at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Lieutenant Colonel Uros Nikolic made a statement which is in tab 382. Was he one of your subordinate officers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was my commander, the commander of the 1st Battalion, and his task was from the Mala Krusa-Pirane axis through the villages of Zojic, Medvedice to fire on -- in the direction of Mamusa, to the west of Mamusa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is contained in his statement? Does it correspond to what you know about these events?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This commander kept me informed regularly from the preparations for action at regular time intervals about the events taking place on his axis. And he mentions this in his statement, that throughout the day, although our forces had already passed this area, a group of terrorists, probably from the village of Neprebiste, making sure of these streams here in the area of the village of Pirane, attacked our supplies unit. And in the area close to Pirane near the mosque in that part of the village there was combat and reserve forces had to be used. Reinforcements were sought in order to help this unit and break up this large terrorist group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the strength of these KLA forces in this area?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a group numbering up to 20 men, and they probably planned to pull out from that axis and break through over the asphalt road and set out towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic, in document 383, also made a statement about these events. Does this statement correspond entirely to what you know from that time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He moved along another route. His statement does correspond. It was his units that emerged at Retimlje and Randubrava villages and his subordinate commanders also gave statements in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under tab 384, Colonel Stojan Konjlkovac also provided a statement describing all the main elements of these events, the actions, that is, of these units in the period the 25th to 28th March.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But he was on a completely different axis. We haven't mentioned him before. He was commander of Combat Group 4, which acted from Suva Reka towards Studencani along this road. His assignment was to link up with the forces of Combat Group 6 and to open up this road for traffic. At this time, he was in the area of Studencani and Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything noteworthy in his statement regarding actions in this area?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 25th, due to the strong resistance put up to his forces, his unit did not manage to advance more than 500 metres and they practically stayed in the same positions up to the 26th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the strength of the KLA opposing them?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the forces which we had reckoned with, he was attacked by other forces from Dobrodeljane village, the Grab feature, and some other forces that came to back them up, from Malisevo and Pagarusa, so that the enemy forces were very strong and he was unable to advance before the 26th along his axis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 385 - I'm trying to move through these documents as fast as I can - we have the statement of Lieutenant Zoran Zjakic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His road was a bit different. Here in the area of Orahovac-Velika Hoca road, he with his combat group were striving to link up with Combat Group 5, under Commander Konjlkovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under tab 386, we have the statement of Colonel Vladimir Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was my Chief of Staff and my deputy. And in the relevant period, he had formed Combat Group 7 as a temporary unit. And along this same route, near Velika Hoca, between Combat Groups 6 and 2 was where he was active.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the penultimate paragraph of his statement, he says: "No movement of civilians was observed during combat. That is, there were no civilians in the village because the Siptar terrorist forces had evacuated them out of the village and dominant features earlier."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians could not be seen. I, for instance, was situated at a very dominant -- dominating elevation, which gave me a very good view. And I could see some columns.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I was unable to see any columns of civilians either on foot or in vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under tab 387, we have the statement of Lieutenant Colonel Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Radivoj Paravinja. Is it also consistent with the previous statements, and in 388 we have the statement of Major Sel Janos.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paravinja intervened twice during the 25th, once towards Landovica and the second when our supply column was attacked on the road. He had no other particular combat assignment except to be on the blocking line and to link up other forces and to command them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is also the subject of the statement of Major Sel Janos under tab 388 and also of the statement of Captain Feta Elifat in 389. Are these statements also consistent with the other ones?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Elifat Feta was in command of some of these units and he -- or rather, Sel Janos was in command of one of these units. He entered these units -- these villages. And Elifat Feta was backup and, according to the orders of the commander, he was behind the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In tab 390, we have the statement of Captain Milovan Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also one of the commanders from the 2nd Motorised Battalion. He was in command of an infantry platoon -- a rifle platoon, rather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under tab 391, we have another statement of yours.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my statement for -- concerning the 26th, and there is also a map showing the operations of the 26th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this statement of yours also concern Landovica and the events of the 26th you have already spoken about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us clarify the number. Is it right that tab 391 contains map and 39 -- tab 392 is statements? Since I have no translation of that statement, I cannot confirm that right now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. 392 is a statement of General Delic, who is here in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is the substance of this statement, in the briefest possible terms?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement describes all the developments as of the 26th, everything that was reported to me, what I was doing as the commander, and all the reports I received from my subordinate commanders. On the 26th, I arrived at my post because on the 25th, as I already explained, I went to see the barracks that had been bombed, to see if all the equipment had been evacuated. And on the 26th at 0600 hours I returned to my command post. I'm trying to be as brief as I can. I was informed of the problem in Landovica around 1700 hours. I ordered -- or rather, I was informed a little after 1000 hours. At 1300 hours there was an airstrike. First cluster bombs were used and then rockets were fired at my unit. Two of my soldiers were wounded, because my soldiers were using the trenches previously abandoned by the terrorists.
