Certain problems occurred in those units that suffered losses, so that I had to go to see that unit and leave my command post. I called one platoon from the reserve force. I pulled out one unit that had suffered casualties. I pulled out one unit from combat to give them time to rest. And I personally accompanied the reserve units when they continued operations along the road, trying to link up with Colonel Konjlkovac, who was attacking from Suva Reka, before dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was this an instance of coordinated action between NATO Air Force and KLA on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way. Although, we lived that a bit this way: The unit that was in actual contact was a couple of hundred metres away. This way only my forces were under strike. Otherwise, they would have been attacked by terrorists as well. But yes, you could call it coordinated action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under 393 we have the statement of Lieutenant Colonel Uros Nikolic, but could you please explain this: He says in the fourth paragraph: "Because it was a clearing, most of the units were exposed to sniper fire from the direction of Donje Retimlje." Was this the usual way that our units would be targeted, from that distance?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Machine-gun fire and often mortar fire, and sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In 394, we have the statement of Colonel Vlatko Vukovic, referring to the same period. There are references to Retimlje, the farm in Retimlje, combat against terrorist forces that lasted until 1700 hours, considerable resistance from the outskirts of the village and from the mosque. It says: "There was no civilian population in the village. Search detected a lot of weapons and ammunition."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the deployment of forces that we had at the time, we could not cover this village because the forces commanded by Colonel Vukovic was constantly under fire by terrorists. And only when Major Sel managed to approach the village from the north, from a direction where they did not have fortified positions, and only when he attacked their flank did their resistance weaken, so that Colonel Vukovic was able to advance with his unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says: "There was no civilian population in the village at the time." Is that something that features in all of these events, where significant forces of the KLA were encountered? There was no civilian population. Is that some sort of rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's a leading question. Perhaps it could be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. Milosevic. Oh, Mr. Saxon, I think he's -- he's citing something. It's a -- it's a reference to -- to what is in the statement. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, General, in the most general terms: As far as all of these events are concerned that your commanders were testifying about, that you testified about, to what extent was the civilian population present in these areas where there was fighting with members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for these specific villages, since the command was there of this brigade and a hospital and all other structures, there was absolutely no civilian population there. They had already left in different directions. What was characteristic, though, was that where there were civilians, the civilian population, as in 1998, it never waited for the army. It was only later that we would find civilian population. We thought that the civilian population would follow the KLA and that then at convenient spots the KLA would go their own way leaving the civilian population behind. That is why we could not operate. Although, sometimes we would see them only a couple of hundred metres in front of us, the terrorists withdrawing from certain positions, but they would have the civilian population with them and in a way they were a human shield, in view of our operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of your unit ever fire at members of the KLA when there could be civilian casualties, when the civilian population could be hurt?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders from 1998, which were valid until the end of the war, absolutely prohibited that because, for example, if the artillery were to fire, there would be a great many civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Never mind what the orders prohibit. What we're interested in is what actually happened. So the question was whether any of your forces ever fired on civilians. And I understand you to be saying no. Mr. Milosevic, your case seems to be this: Where the indictment alleges crimes committed by forces of the FRY and Serbia, you're either saying that they were not involved at all in any incidents as alleged, as in Bijela Crkva, or if they were involved, then they were participating in a lawful exercise to root out KLA terrorists and that they used no more force than was reasonably necessary in doing so, and further, at no time did they ever target civilians. Would that be a summary of your case in relation to all these allegations in the Kosovo indictment where it is alleged that forces of the FRY and Serbia committed certain crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. The witness can also answer that question, whether that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. No. He's -- no, I'm asking you if that -- if this is your case, if that is the defence you're putting forward, not the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is what is true, and that is what is the entire body of knowledge about what had happened. That is true. That is correct. You defined it very well. I asked the general not what the orders were. The orders are well known. I asked him whether any one of his units - and you can check that on the transcript - fired at forces if there were civilians there. I'm asking him what happened in fact, what the orders were. The orders are well known. I asked him that question, seeking an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As briefly as possible, the forces never opened fire. The artillery never opened fire on the terrorists, if civilians were with them, women, children, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you mentioned in some cases where your soldiers shot civilians who were after prosecuted for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But they did not use artillery pieces to open that fire. And artillery is being discussed now. These are soldiers who directly killed some civilians using their very own weapons at close range. Now we are talking about artillery support. Whether sometimes we used artillery, mortars to fire at areas where there were terrorists and civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, please bear in mind that practically every description contained in Mr. Nice's accusations starts with the statement that "The forces of the FRY and Serbia shelled a village, surrounded a village, shelled it, and then entered the village, looted it, and burned it." The General's area of responsibility is very big, as you can see, and he claimed that kind of thing never happened, that somebody indiscriminately shelled a village, that civilians were killed, and then that they barged into the village looting, killing, torching, et cetera. His testimony is quite clear, and it is corroborated and supported by documents and statements by commanding officers from his unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: His testimony as I understand it is that in most cases these villages had KLA forces entrenched.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His testimony was that in the villages where the army intervened there were KLA forces. You saw the example of Bijela Crkva. There were no KLA forces there, and the army went through Bijela Crkva. Where the army was fired at, where there were fortified positions on the outskirts of the village, then the army did fire at the KLA. That is what the General was explaining. So as far as villages where there was no action against the army were concerned, they were not touched. Villages that were used for firing at the army were treated in a selective manner, and it was only the firing positions that fired at the army that were engaged. That is completely legitimate action, as far as the military is concerned. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, thank you. We'll adjourn now and resume on Tuesday, the 5th at 9.00 a.m.
